name: Mini facelift (S-lift)

card.summary: A short-scar facelift using small incisions near the ear, usually without neck work; lighter recovery, and Wikipedia describes the result as more temporary.
card.note: Suited by surgeons' accounts to early laxity; evidence is surgeon series, with few head-to-head comparisons.

quick.overview:
The mini facelift, often called the S-lift or short-scar facelift, uses shorter incisions around the ear than a traditional facelift and generally omits neck lifting. It is described as suiting people with early jowling or modest sagging and a firm neck.

Surgeons describe less dramatic change and shorter recovery. Wikipedia describes the effect as more temporary than full facelifts. A 2007 review noted that studies comparing facelift methods are few.
quick.mechanism: The S-lift suspends sagging tissue using a strong permanent purse-string suture and a short skin flap, with incisions in front of and below the ear shaped like an S.
quick.risks: Facelift risks in general include hematoma, nerve injury, scarring and hair loss at incisions. Combining the S-lift with laser resurfacing has been reported in retrospective series with side effect profiles described by authors.

lead: The mini facelift is a family of short-scar rhytidectomy techniques, commonly called the S-lift, that use limited incisions and omit the neck lift. Wikipedia says it suits people with deep nasolabial folds and sagging but a firm, well-contoured neck, has less downtime, and may be done endoscopically; it describes the result as more temporary.[1]

An S-lift was described in the literature in 1999 and is based on suspending sagging facial features with a strong permanent purse-string suture, according to the authors of a 2002 paper who then proposed a modification, the minimal access cranial suspension (MACS) lift.[2] A 2001 dermatologic surgery paper describes an S-lift using U-suture and O-suture combined with skin resurfacing, suggesting it may help minor jowling or submental laxity in early ptosis or revision facelifts.[3]
Reports are mainly surgeon-authored. A 2007 review of facelift techniques noted that few studies compare results between methods.[4]

paras: Mini lifts use short incisions, limited skin elevation and often a purse-string or plication suture to reposition tissue, rather than extensive dissection of deeper layers.[1][2] Variants include the S-Plus lift, a short-scar long-flap rhytidectomy,[5] and mini rhytidectomy techniques published since the 1990s, including one adapted for Asian patients.[6][7]

Authors of a 2002 paper reported a trend toward less dramatic facial rejuvenation, noting patients wanted improvement without prolonged disfigurement or high complication risk, and that the S-lift had been described in 1999.[2] A 1997 article on the mini rhytidectomy and a 2005 overview of S-lift and S-Plus lift rhytidectomies document the spread of the concept.[6][8]
Retrospective analyses have examined surgical lifting combined with ablative laser resurfacing in the same session, reporting results and side effects.[9]
Facelift complications in general include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and hair loss; smoking raises risk.[1]

Evidence is surgeon-reported. The 2002 MACS paper and the 2001 S-lift paper describe technique and outcomes in case series.[2][3] A 2010 article reports on the S-Plus lift.[5] A 2007 review concludes that comparisons between methods are limited.[4] No randomized trials were found.

timeline.event: MACS lift proposed as a modified S-lift.[2]
S-Plus lift, a short-scar long-flap technique, reported.[5]
